others.C: Provisioning EC2 and ELB only at failover time (pilot light) adds minutes of recovery time.
others.D: A 10-minute CloudWatch evaluation plus a Lambda DNS update is slower and more fragile than Route 53 health-check failover.

tip: DR strategies from slowest to fastest: backup and restore, pilot light, warm standby, multi-site active/active.

why: An S3 gateway endpoint gives instances in a private subnet private access to S3 over the AWS network through route-table entries, at no additional charge. It is the most cost-effective way to keep the traffic off the public internet.

others.A: A NAT gateway sends traffic to S3's public endpoints and charges hourly and per GB.
others.B: Storage Gateway is for on-premises access to AWS storage, not EC2-to-S3 connectivity.
others.C: An interface endpoint also works privately but costs hourly and per GB, unlike the free gateway endpoint.

tip: From inside the VPC the gateway endpoint is the cheapest S3 path. Interface endpoints are for on-premises or cross-Region access.

why: The application uses the transport layer (Layer 4, TCP/UDP), so a Network Load Balancer fits it. An Auto Scaling group spanning multiple AZs with health checks replaces failed instances and spreads capacity across AZs. The NLB in front sends traffic only to healthy targets, giving cost-effective high availability.

others.A: Route 53 DNS routing to instances is slower to react to failures and still needs manual instance management, with no self-healing.
others.C: Adding an ALB as well is unnecessary cost; the app is Layer 4 and one NLB is enough.
others.E: Restarting stopped instances in one AZ does not protect against an AZ failure.

tip: Layer 4 means NLB. Layer 7 (HTTP) means ALB. High availability means Multi-AZ Auto Scaling with health checks.

why: With fewer than 100 visits a month, API Gateway plus Lambda costs effectively nothing (pay per request, mostly within the free tier) and needs no servers. One Lambda function serves or handles the form, and another publishes to an SNS topic with an email subscription, so the company gets an email for each submission. This is the most cost-effective serverless design.

others.A: An ECS service running all the time costs far more than needed for 100 visits a month, and SES does not need a third-party provider.
others.C: SQS is a queue and cannot deliver email notifications, and the Amplify server-side setup adds unnecessary components.
others.D: Windows EC2 with IIS runs all the time and costs much more, and WorkMail is a mailbox service, not a notification mechanism.

tip: Very low, sporadic traffic means serverless pay-per-request (API Gateway, Lambda, SNS or SES).

why: Pointing root user emails to company-controlled aliases that land in a centrally secured mailbox means no individual owns root recovery, and important root notices are not missed. Setting AWS alternate contacts for billing, operations and security to dedicated, business-managed distribution lists routes each notification category to the right team, which is the most secure and controlled approach.

others.A: A single shared mailbox that all account owners can access spreads root email access widely, weakening root account security.
others.B: Separate per-business-unit lists that include administrators widen who can receive root password-reset emails and duplicate management.
others.C: Tying a root email to one individual creates a single point of failure and risk if that person leaves.

tip: Use alternate contacts (billing, operations, security) for notification routing. Keep root email on a secured, centrally controlled address.

why: Putting purchase requests on an SQS queue decouples intake from processing, so spikes are buffered instead of timing out. An Auto Scaling group of workers, which can scale on queue depth, processes messages at a sustainable rate. ElastiCache in front of Aurora serves repeated reads such as product data, cutting database load cheaply.

others.A: Retrying purchases from extra instances adds load during peaks. RDS Proxy helps with connection pooling but does not buffer demand.
others.D: A Lambda function that keeps retrying purchases increases pressure on the database instead of smoothing it.
others.E: API Gateway usage plans throttle clients, which rejects customers rather than scaling to meet peak demand.

tip: Timeouts at peak usually mean decouple with SQS plus worker scaling, and cache reads.

why: Amazon Athena can query Cost and Usage Report data stored in S3 directly (AWS provides Athena integration for CUR). Amazon QuickSight uses Athena as a data source to build and share a custom dashboard of daily NAT gateway costs month-to-date with senior leadership.

others.A: DataSync is a data transfer service and cannot act as a query engine for QuickSight.
others.C: CloudWatch dashboards do not query CUR files, and DataSync cannot run queries.
others.D: CloudWatch dashboards cannot use Athena to query CUR data for custom cost tables.

tip: Custom cost dashboards from CUR mean CUR in S3, queried with Athena, shown in QuickSight (for example the CUDOS dashboards).

why: A CloudFront default TTL of 2 minutes caches objects without Cache-Control headers briefly, so content is never more than a few minutes stale. For objects with a long max-age (24 hours), an invalidation on each deployment removes changed files from edge caches immediately. Together these give good cache hit rates without stale content after deployments.

others.B: S3 buckets have no TTL setting; TTLs are set in CloudFront or through object Cache-Control headers.
others.C: Cache-Control: private stops CloudFront from caching, which defeats the performance goal.
others.D: An Expires header added on viewer response affects only browser caching, not CloudFront edge caching, and adds Lambda@Edge cost.

tip: For CloudFront freshness, use TTLs or Cache-Control max-age plus invalidations (or versioned file names) on deploy.

why: A Compute Savings Plan covers EC2 and Lambda (and Fargate) usage, so it discounts both the instances and the growing Lambda usage for the 1-year term. Attaching the Lambda functions to the same VPC private subnets gives them direct private network access to the EC2 instances.

others.A: An EC2 Instance Savings Plan does not cover Lambda, so the growing Lambda costs stay at full price.
others.B: An EC2 Instance Savings Plan does not cover Lambda, and Lambda functions in public subnets do not get public IPs, so there is no benefit.
others.D: Functions in the Lambda service VPC cannot reach private EC2 instances in the customer VPC.

tip: Savings Plans: Compute covers EC2, Fargate and Lambda. EC2 Instance covers only EC2 in one family and Region. SageMaker has its own plan.

why: AWS Budgets can track each developer account with alerts on actual and forecasted spend. Budget actions can automatically apply an IAM policy, such as DenyAll, or an SCP when the threshold is reached, which enforces the limit with no custom code. This gives the least operational overhead.

others.A: Tagging rules, custom termination Lambda functions and daily reports are complex and depend on developers' cooperation.
others.C: Cost Explorer reports and Anomaly Detection only inform; they do not limit spending.
others.D: Service Catalog plus custom start and stop Lambda functions in every account adds significant overhead and does not cap costs.

tip: To enforce a spending limit automatically, use AWS Budgets actions (apply an IAM policy or SCP, or stop EC2/RDS instances).

why: Least-privilege chaining uses security group references between tiers. The web tier accepts HTTPS only from the ALB's security group. The app tier accepts HTTPS only from the web tier's security group. The database tier accepts SQL Server traffic (TCP 1433) only from the app tier's security group. Security groups are stateful, so return traffic is allowed automatically.

others.B: Outbound HTTPS from the web tier to 0.0.0.0/0 is overly broad and unnecessary for tier communication.
others.D: The database should never initiate traffic to the web tier; responses are handled by statefulness.
others.F: The app tier needs no outbound connections to the web tier, and SQL traffic should go to the database tier, not the web tier.

tip: Reference upstream security group IDs as sources for each tier, and rely on statefulness for return traffic.

why: A Compute Savings Plan applies to EC2, Lambda and Fargate in one commitment. SageMaker usage is covered only by a SageMaker Savings Plan. These two plans cover all four services with the fewest plans.

others.A: EC2 Instance Savings Plans cover only EC2 in a specific family and Region, not SageMaker.
others.B: Compute Savings Plans do not cover SageMaker.
others.E: EC2 Instance Savings Plans do not cover Fargate.

tip: Compute Savings Plans cover EC2, Fargate and Lambda. SageMaker needs a separate SageMaker Savings Plan.

why: Babelfish for Aurora PostgreSQL understands the SQL Server wire protocol (TDS) and T-SQL, so applications keep their existing queries and drivers with minimal code change. SCT (or the Babelfish Compass assessment) and DMS move the schema and data into Aurora PostgreSQL.

others.A: Rewriting application SQL contradicts the minimal-code-change goal. SCT converts database schema and code, not application query rewriting at scale.
others.D: RDS Proxy pools connections but does not translate T-SQL or the SQL Server protocol.
others.E: DMS migrates data and does not rewrite application SQL queries.

tip: SQL Server to Aurora PostgreSQL with minimal app changes means Babelfish.

why: EBS encryption by default is an account-level, per-Region EC2 setting. Once enabled, every new EBS volume and snapshot copy is encrypted automatically with the default or chosen KMS key, and unencrypted volumes cannot be created. It satisfies both requirements with one setting.

others.B: The AWS Config encrypted-volumes rule only detects unencrypted volumes after creation; it does not prevent or encrypt them.
others.C: Creating encrypted copies with Systems Manager is a reactive manual workflow that does not stop unencrypted creation.
others.D: Migration Hub tracks migrations and does not enforce EBS encryption.

tip: EBS encryption by default is set per Region, so enable it in every Region you use. Combine it with SCPs (ec2:Encrypted) for extra enforcement.

why: Kinesis Data Streams in on-demand mode automatically scales shard capacity with fluctuating throughput, so there is no capacity planning. Lambda's Kinesis event source mapping processes records in near real time and scales with the stream, giving a fully elastic clickstream pipeline.

others.B: Firehose buffers data for delivery (seconds to minutes), and Glue is a batch or streaming ETL service, not ideal for this real-time per-event processing.
others.C: Kinesis Video Streams is for video and media streams, not clickstream events.
others.D: Managed Service for Apache Flink processes streams; it is not an ingestion endpoint for capturing data from websites.

tip: Unpredictable streaming throughput means Kinesis Data Streams on-demand mode.

why: S3 Storage Lens gives organization-wide, multi-Region visibility of S3, including data protection metrics such as the count of buckets with versioning enabled. Drilling down identifies buckets without versioning, with no custom tooling.

others.A: CloudTrail records API events; it cannot list the current versioning state of existing buckets.
others.C: IAM Access Analyzer for S3 reports public or cross-account access, not versioning status.
others.D: Multi-Region Access Points route requests across Regions and do not audit bucket configuration.

tip: An AWS Config s3-bucket-versioning-enabled rule (with an aggregator) is another valid way to find these buckets.

why: After 30 days the files are rarely accessed but must still be retrievable immediately. S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval gives millisecond access at about 68% lower storage cost than Standard-IA, and the files are large enough (5 MB) that its 128 KB minimum and 90-day minimum do not matter. An expiration action deletes the files after 4 years.

others.B: One Zone-IA keeps data in a single AZ, which is risky for files that cannot be recreated, and it costs more than Glacier Instant Retrieval for rarely accessed data.
others.C: Standard-IA provides immediate access but costs more per GB than Glacier Instant Retrieval for rarely accessed data.
others.D: Moving files to Glacier Flexible Retrieval at 4 years is wrong, because the files should be deleted then, and Standard-IA costs more in the meantime.

tip: Rarely accessed, needs millisecond access, kept for months or years means S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval.

why: S3 Multi-Region Access Points provide a single global endpoint that routes requests over the AWS global network (through AWS Global Accelerator) to the closest bucket, avoiding public internet congestion. In active-active mode with Cross-Region Replication keeping buckets in sync, failover is automatic and needs very little S3 management.

others.A: Making the application choose Regional endpoints means custom routing and failover logic, and traffic uses the public internet.
others.B: A Multi-Region Access Point has one global endpoint, not one per Region, and active-passive does not send users to the nearest bucket.
others.C: Cross-account replication is not the issue, and Regional endpoints do not avoid internet congestion or give automatic failover.

tip: A single global S3 endpoint with routing to the nearest bucket and failover means Multi-Region Access Points plus CRR.

why: An Auto Scaling group with minimum and maximum of 1, launched from each app's AMI (and spanning multiple AZ subnets), keeps exactly one instance running. It automatically replaces the instance in a healthy AZ if it fails ELB health checks, giving self-healing reliability without changing the legacy apps. This suits apps that cannot run as multiple concurrent instances.

others.B: Hourly backups with manual restores give slow recovery and possible data loss, so they are not fault tolerant.
others.C: Running two active instances may break legacy apps that were not designed for concurrency or shared state, which would require design changes.
others.D: Refactoring into containers violates the 'no design changes' constraint (and the service is Migration Hub Refactor Spaces).

tip: An ASG with min = max = 1 is the standard self-healing pattern for single-instance legacy applications.

why: AWS Control Tower Account Factory creates accounts with preventive and detective guardrails automatically. A central networking account that owns a VPC and shares its subnets with workload accounts through AWS RAM (VPC sharing) centralizes network management while each workload stays isolated in its own account.

others.B: Plain AWS Organizations account creation does not apply guardrails automatically.
others.C: A VPC in every account plus transit gateway and inspection routing is more networking to manage than sharing central subnets.
others.D: Organizations alone has no automatic guardrails, and per-account VPCs with a transit gateway add overhead.

tip: Central networking for many accounts means VPC sharing through RAM. Automatic guardrails mean Control Tower.

why: Static content does not need EC2 or an ALB. Hosting it in S3 with CloudFront in front removes server costs, scales automatically, and caches at edge locations. With Origin Access Control and CloudFront's lower egress pricing, costs stay low as traffic grows.

others.B: ElastiCache cannot sit in front of S3 for web serving, and it adds cluster costs.
others.C: An ALB in front of Amplify is unnecessary and adds cost; Amplify already provides hosting and a CDN.
others.D: EC2 caching instances bring back the server costs the company wants to remove.

tip: Static website at the lowest cost means S3 plus CloudFront.

why: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server is a fully managed native Windows file system with SMB support, Active Directory integration, Multi-AZ options and automatic backups. Application servers connect over SMB with no servers to manage, giving the least administrative overhead.

others.A: Volume Gateway provides iSCSI block volumes, not SMB file shares, and is meant for hybrid on-premises use.
others.B: Tape Gateway provides a virtual tape library for backup software, not shared SMB storage.
others.C: A self-managed Windows file server on EC2 needs patching, backups and HA work.

tip: SMB in AWS means FSx for Windows File Server (or FSx for NetApp ONTAP). NFS for Linux means EFS.

why: Aurora Global Database replicates storage to the secondary Region with typically under 1 second of lag, far inside the 5-minute RPO. A managed planned switchover or failover promotes us-west-1 in minutes, well inside the 20-minute RTO. Converting an existing cluster to a global database needs no application or schema changes, and the global writer endpoint keeps configuration changes minimal.

others.A: A cross-Region Aurora MySQL read replica uses binlog replication with higher lag and requires manual promotion, which is less efficient.
others.C: 'Cross-Region Replication' for a new standalone cluster is effectively binlog replication with manual failover and more configuration.
others.D: DMS-based sync is self-managed, has higher lag and adds operational overhead.

tip: Cross-Region Aurora DR with an RPO of seconds and an RTO of about a minute means Aurora Global Database.
